speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always very difficult to express oneself adequately when a fellow member passes from this scene. Last evening all of us were deeply shocked at the sudden passing of Mr. J. Omer Gour, member for Russell. I had just left the house a few moments before, and on arrival at my office was informed that he had joined the group who in the service of their country pass away. He was a man of genial disposition, kindly in his relationship with his fellow members and one who without exaggeration did have the affection of all who served with him, irrespective of political persuasion.
He came into the House of Commons in 1945, having already established for himself an intimate connection with the lives of the people of his constituency. He was an executive in a number of co-operatives and was greatly interested in agriculture. He had given himself to public service in various charitable and semi-public institutions in his

community. He had served as mayor of his home town of Casselman for a period of five years. Indeed, his wide interests in the community are spelled out in the list of organizations to which he gave the benefit of his advice and to which he made a contribution.
Here in the House of Commons in a most gentle manner he epitomized those characteristics of public service which are the hallmark of good citizenship. He looked upon his membership in the House of Commons as an opportunity for greater personal service to the people of his constituency who sought his counsel at all times. Indeed, as I remember it, when he had his first office on the first floor of this building the numbers who came to him for advice were so great that he had to establish, as it were, an additional office in the hallway. He was a good member. I speak as one who liked him because of his infinite fairness and his attitude in general to the discussion of public affairs.
On behalf of the government and the people of Canada I wish to extend our deepest sympathy to his widow, his two daughters and his son. To them I trust will come the comfort that is felt by those who, having lost a loved one, realize that his service and the contribution he made to his constituency, his province and his country will be a monument in the years ahead to that life of service. I want to add as well the sympathy of my colleagues, myself and members on the government side of the house to the Leader of the Opposition and his colleagues in the great loss that he and they have sustained in the passing of one who enjoyed the affection of the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the Prime Minister for what he has said about our friend and colleague. We are reminded by his words that within a week a second seat in the House of Commons has been vacated by sudden death. Once again last evening we were shocked into a realization of the transient and uncertain character of man's life and man's affairs.
We in this house have lost in the death of Mr. Gour one of our senior members, a member with 15 years of service in the house. As the Prime Minister has said, Mr. Gour reached the House of Commons after many years of

Tributes to Deceased Members public service in his own community and after achieving success in his own field of private activity.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, the measure of a man's worth is best judged from the feeling for him by the people among whom he lived and worked. In the case of Joe Gour that feeling was one of respect and affection for a man whose whole life was one of service to others. That same feeling, I know, was shared by all his fellow members in the house, particularly perhaps by those of us who worked with him in the Liberal party and who deeply appreciated his unselfish and complete co-operation and his wise counsel, expressed always with modesty but with frankness and sometimes with a saltiness that caused it to be remembered.
He was a strong party man, but his friendships in the house were not limited by party affiliations as happily is so often the case. We all liked him. He was a good and modest man. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, he was always fair and ever generous in his assessment of policies, with a particular interest in how they affected his farmers, his people as he always called them. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I think it is true to say that he had become a notable parliamentary personality over the years he was in the house, one who had earned and had received our regard and our affection. We shall all miss him greatly.
I join with the Prime Minister in his expression of deep sympathy to Mrs. Gour and the members of the family at this dark time. Their loss was as sudden as it is irreparable.

Mr. Speaker, the passing of Mr. Gour last evening demonstrates once again to all members of the house how fleeting and temporary is our life. I was particularly shocked because I have had the good fortune for some time to sit in the house next to him. We became close friends, and I cannot speak too highly of his personal qualities.
As has already been said, he came to this house in 1945. In parliament and in his community he worked in the interests of agriculture. He worked in his community in the interests of community life and in the interests of his church. I have admired Mr. Gour and his activities in parliament for many years because of his fairness, and because of his independent turn of mind. I can remember a number of occasions on which he spoke out most forthrightly on controversial issues. He was a man who felt, in one instance, that his government should move in the field of interest rates in order to protect the incomes of the ordinary people of this country.

He was a member of the agriculture committee, as I have been, for many years. I can agree with the statement by the Leader of the Opposition that he had the interests of the farmers, the people of his constituency, very close to his heart. We know that in parliament he worked under something of a handicap. I think, with the handicap he had, he showed great bravery in always being prepared to stand up and speak his mind in the interests of justice as he saw it.
I join with the Prime Minister in extending to the Leader of the Opposition and to the Liberal party our sympathy at the loss of a valuable colleague. We extend to Mrs. Gour and to the three children our most sincere sympathy.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it does not happen too often in parliamentary life that a member has to interrupt his speech to be informed of the demise of a colleague. That was my experience last night, while I was speaking to a resolution relating to the Department of Transport.
As soon as the house adjourned, I went to my fellow-member's office, where I witnessed a very moving scene. The party whip, surrounded by our colleagues, was reciting prayers until the arrival of the priest who later administered the last sacraments, while our colleague's widow and his two children could not believe that their husband and father was no more.
Mr. Speaker, Joseph Gour had great virtues. He was a good and generous man. Many people in his riding and elsewhere frequently benefited from his generosity.
He was a most sincere man, faithful to his principles. On many occasions he fearlessly made his views known on difficult and delicate matters. Only recently, as my colleagues in the house well know, at a farmer's meeting where some of us had been speaking in general terms, Joseph Gour did not hesitate to express his opinion bluntly so that the farmers might fully know and understand exactly what he had in mind.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, Joseph Gour was a party man. That is not a bad thing. It only proves, as the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said a moment ago, that one can be a party man and still deserve the respect, friendship and affection of members, not only on the opposition but also on the government side.
When I was member for Stormont, Mr. Gour was my neighbour and, on several occasions, came to my constituency to give me a hand.

The two tragic events which have occurred in the house within a week, should, it seems to me, teach us a lesson. On one side of the house there was a member who had achieved great things, both in the national and international fields, while on this side, another member's activity is abruptly ended after he, too, had done great things in a more restricted field, his district, his constituency. Both, however, are of equal status before their Maker and I feel that, whatever our qualities, successes, shortcomings or failures, each and everyone of us should remember that we are all equal in the eyes of the ultimate Judge.
Mr. Speaker, Joseph Gour was a patriot. He loved French, he loved French education and culture, and hardly missed an opportunity to speak in their behalf, especially when they stood for the advancement of his own people in Ontario. I am sure that no member of the house, even among those who do not share my views in this regard, will begrudge my saying that, because of that attitude, he has been of genuine service to his constituents.
Then too, and above all, Joseph Gour was a family man. He loved and adored his wife, children and grandchildren, and lived for them. His passing will create a great void among us, but in his family that void will never be filled.
To his bereaved widow, to his son Robert and to his daughters Gaby and Raymonde we extend our deepest sympathy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to acquaint the house with the government's proposals with reference to the terms of union with Newfoundland.
Article 29 of the terms of union provided as follows:
Review of Financial Position 29. In view of the difficulty of predicting with sufficient accuracy the financial consequences to Newfoundland of becoming a province of Canada, the government of Canada will appoint a royal commission within eight years from the date of union to review the financial position of the province of Newfoundland and to recommend the form and scale of additional financial assistance, if any, that may he required by the government of the province of Newfoundland to enable it to continue public services at the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union, without resort-66968-9-140J
Newfoundland Terms of Union ing to taxation more burdensome, having regard to capacity to pay, than that obtaining generally in the region comprising the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island.
In pursuance of this provision the former government appointed a royal commission consisting of Chief Justice McNair of New Brunswick, the late Sir Albert Walsh, chief justice of Newfoundland, and Mr. John Deutsch. Their report was submitted not long before prorogation of the last session of this parliament, and by that report they recommended that Canada should pay to Newfoundland additional financial assistance after the transitional grants as follows:

The recommendations of the royal commission have been studied with care and were discussed by the government with the premier and other representatives of the government of Newfoundland. Both governments have entertained serious reservations concerning the basis of the conclusions reached by the commissioners. We in particular have been concerned that the commissioners have used the fiscal year 1957-58 as the base year, whereas the period accepted as the basis in the presentation of all the evidence was the fiscal year 1956-57, which accords with the terms of article 29 which I read in full a moment ago. The vague nature of the commissioners' recommendation as to the duration of the payments has also occasioned difficulty for both governments. In his final submission to the royal commission, counsel for Newfoundland argued quite specifically that provision should be made for a further review of the economic and financial position of the province within a reasonable period of time. The government of the province still asserts that position as the proper interpretation of the rather uncertain and nebulous provisions of article 29.
Since the fiscal year 1957-58, and incidentally since this government came into power, Newfoundland has greatly benefited from additional forms of financial assistance from the government of Canada. The new direct payments alone aggregated over $9 million in the fiscal year 1958-59. This amount included the increased rate of standard individual income tax, the higher than average per capita benefit extended to Newfoundland through the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, as well as various increased or new conditional grants.

Newfoundland Terms of Union
Notwithstanding the difficulties presented by its report, it remains a fact that the royal commission was appointed to fulfil the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada, and these terms are part of the British North America Act. My colleagues and I are accordingly of the opinion that parliament should be invited to take action on the commission's recommendations. It is proposed, therefore, to ask parliament to authorize payments as recommended by the royal commission, but in our view the duration of the payments should be limited to five years, as both Newfoundland and Canada have recognized the difficulties involved in making projections from one selected year into the future, and it has further appeared to be quite inappropriate to endeavour to provide for a fixed amount payable annually over a period of unlimited duration. A resolution will shortly be placed on the order paper asking leave to introduce a bill to carry into effect these provisions pertaining to the terms of union. The proposed payments will be unconditional and will be in final and irrevocable settlement of the provisions of article 29 and the contractual obligations of the union consummated in 1949.
On conclusion of the payments as of March 31, 1962, which corresponds with the conclusion of the present five-year fiscal arrangement between Canada and the provinces, Newfoundland's position can be considered in the light of the general methods of providing financial assistance to the provinces which may be in effect at that time.
Provision will be made in the bill for the payment to Newfoundland of the amounts due for 1957-58 and 1958-59, totalling $13,550,000, before the government accounts are closed for the present fiscal year.
I should now like to say a word respecting the 10th anniversary of the union of Newfoundland with Canada, which will be celebrated next Wednesday, April 1. As the house will not be sitting then may I be allowed on behalf of Canadians in the other nine provinces to convey to the people of Newfoundland the pride we all feel in the decision then made whereby they became Canadians.
Each of the provinces has its problems, and Newfoundland is no exception. Differences do exist as to the solution of these problems; but my certain faith, based on the achievements of the past, is that these differences will be solved in the spirit of confederation and with that understanding and common dedication that are the enduring basis of confederation.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS NEWFOUNDLAND'    STATEMENT ON REVISION OF TERMS OF UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's statement indicates that the government will
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
ask parliament to discharge an obligation to Newfoundland, one which arises out of the terms of union with that province and one which was examined by a royal commission which made certain recommendations in regard to its discharge. I suggest that any additional forms of financial assistance which may have been given to Newfoundland since that royal commission reported or indeed before it reported have no bearing whatever on this particular contractual constitutional obligation.
I welcomed, as I am sure all hon. members of the house welcomed, the statement of the Prime Minister that action is to be recommended in the terms of the royal commission report in so far as the amount of financial assistance is concerned. I regret that this was not done many months ago, whereby the uncertainty which had been created by this delay could have been avoided, and I think the government is to be criticized for not having taken this action earlier.
I hope I am not misinterpreting what the Prime Minister said when I note that this assistance is to be for five years only. That does not seem to me to be compatible with the obligation which the government of Canada accepted in the terms of union. While it is one thing to have these terms re-examined and perhaps reviewed at the end of five years, it is quite another to assume that no obligation will exist after five years. That assumption is quite unwarranted.
The Prime Minister has made reference to the fact that we are approaching the 10th anniversary of the union of Newfoundland with Canada. That was a happy event for all of us at the time it happened, and we can all take great pride in this completion of the work of confederation. The Prime Minister has mentioned that there are difficulties between the province and the central government. We have had difficulties of that kind before in confederation, and I feel certain that with a spirit of good will and understanding-and that means understanding of the situation and circumstances of Newfoundland as well as those of Ottawa- these difficulties can be resolved and that this union between the oldest British colony and Canada will continue to develop and flourish in the years ahead as it has in the past 10 years to the benefit of the people of Newfoundland and of the rest of Canada.

speechtext:
1.	Was there a train derailment on the Canadian National Railways line between Sudbury and Hornepayne on March 20 or March 21, 1959?
2.	If so, what were the particulars, including the location, speed of the train, preliminary estimate of the cause and of the cost of such derailment, the length of time through traffic was held up, and details of train rerouting caused by the derailment?
3.	Has there been a reduction In the maintenance of way personnel in the past 12 months on the section where the derailment took place?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: C.N.R. TRAIN DERAILMENT, SUDBURY-HORNEPAYNE
speechtext:
The answer to part 1 is yes, on March 21.
In regard to part 2, the management advise that super Continental train No. 1 had 13 cars and the diesel unit derailed at mileage 121, Ruel subdivision on the Capreol division. All cars and the diesel unit remained upright, and no personal injuries were suffered. The investigation into the cause of the accident has not yet been completed. Preliminary indications are that the speed of the train was not excessive, and the damage to the equipment was slight and is not expected to exceed $1,000. As a result of the derailment the main track was blocked for approximately 22 hours, and trains were detoured between Austin, on the Sudbury subdivision, and Oba, on the Oba subdivision, over the C.P.R. and Algoma Central and Hudson Bay lines.
As to part 3, there has been no reduction in manpower during the past 12 months in the maintenance of way forces on the section where this derailment took place, and there has been no deterioration in the standard of maintenance of this section of track.
Part 4 is, of course, answered by the answer to part 3.

speechtext:
1.	Has the government received information that certain foreign shipping lines have had subsidies

approved by their governments for service into Canadian ports along the St. Lawrence-great lakes seaway?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: FOREIGN SHIPPING SUBSIDIES, ST. LAWRENCE-GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
The answer to parts 1 and 2 is that it is understood that the United States government has indicated that it proposes to subsidize certain shipping services from United States great lakes ports to Caribbean and trans-Atlantic areas. Since this is a matter of United States decision we do not, as yet, have full information as to what lines and types of service may be involved. I have seen reports that the United States company, Grace Lines, has been authorized to operate on one of these routes but I am not aware that any other companies have as yet been named. In the case of Grace Lines it is understood that the company will be permitted to carry cargo between Canadian great lakes-St. Lawrence ports and foreign ports en route. As I indicated in reply to a previous question, this situation is being watched carefully.
With regard to part 3, this information was given in the answer I made yesterday to the hon. member, namely that the Canada Shipping Act prevents these ships from moving cargo from one Canadian port to another Canadian port.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 24, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Hees-Mr. Rea in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to direct the board of transport commissioners to

require by order the reduction of class and commodity freight rates (other than competitive rates) charged by carriers subject to the order of the board dated November 17, 1958, and to authorize payments to reimburse carriers for the resulting reduction of their revenues up to an aggregate amount of twenty million dollars.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last evening I had just begun to discuss the merits of this resolution when as the house knows I was unfortunately interrupted by an incident which we have all had occasion to regret. At that time, sir, I was discussing the resolution and its implications in so far as the board of transport commissioners' judgment of November 17, 1958 is concerned. I was about to say that the decision in its recital of the facts, which may be found on pages 5 to 7, indicates that the application made to the board stated that the cost of applying the recommendations of the conciliation board to all railway employees in the two-year period from January 1, 1958 to December 31, 1959 would add to rail expenses for the Canadian National Railways $41.5 million, and for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company $26.5 million. As will be seen from the two statements which are to be found on exhibits 58-17 and 58-27, the burden of the judgment is unequally distributed between the two calendar years 1958 and 1959, being respectively $11.5 million and $30 million for the C.N.R., and $7.1 million and $19.2 million for the C.P.R.
The decision, sir, also indicates that the application stated that in order to enable Canadian National Railways to secure full requitement of the additional labour cost would require a general increase in freight rates of 19 per cent, with 25 cents on coal and coke.
Furthermore, the decision of the board sets forth in clear and unequivocal language the facts that entered into its consideration and contains an excellent review of the contention of the various parties to the application as well as a clear consideration of the law and the method followed by the board in the application of these freight rate hearings. It is sufficient, however, for my purposes at this time to say that the board considered that an increase of 17 per cent with 22 cents on coal and coke would yield revenue approximately equivalent to the amount of the Canadian Pacific's additional labour cost and accordingly authorized such increases in freight rates to be made effective on or after December 1, 1958.
During these hearings both the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific railway submitted estimates of additional revenues they would respectively receive from the increases they had applied for and these figures will be found on pages 28 and 29

of the judgment. These figures show by implication the difficulties which the railways expect to encounter in applying an increase in rates. Thus, the statement of the Canadian National Railways on page 29 indicates that on traffic moving under competitive rates, for instance, they expect to earn in 1959 revenues of $73.8 million and to receive from a 19 per cent increase additional revenue of $7,011 million, which are equivalent to an average increase of 9.5 per cent; and the Canadian National Railways expect to earn revenues of $175.1 million from all other freight traffic and to receive from a 19 per cent increase on this traffic a further $25.9 million which is equivalent to an average increase of 14.8 per cent.
In the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway the additional revenues from these two classes of traffic are estimated at amounts equivalent to average increases of 9.5 per cent and 15.2 per cent, the difference between the C.P.R. and C.N.R. percentages being attributable no doubt to different operating conditions.
The clear inference to be drawn from these estimates is that the railways believe on a substantial part of the traffic falling into one or other of these two classes it will not be possible to apply the full amount of the increase authorized. All traffic does not move under the same conditions and in some instances because of competition or because of the harsh realities of economics it is just not possible to impose a higher rate and the traffic simply will not stand for it. This is not merely a debating point, it has greater significance than that. It opens up the enormous if not insuperable difficulties of giving effect to the proposal which the minister has brought before the committee.
These are some of the questions that come to my mind: How is this subsidy to be provided for by the government? How will it be allocated? Where is the formula that will be applied in distributing this subsidy? There was no indication of that given by the minister in his statement and I presume we will not receive that, if at all, until we get the bill.
I believe it is of tremendous importance that before the committee moves on this it knows on what basis, on what formula and by what method the board or the government will apply this subsidy of $20 million. That leads me to submit to the minister and to the committee the following examples.
Let us suppose that of the great volume of traffic moving at class and commodity rates there are three items and that the railways believe that on item A the maximum increase they can apply is 5 per cent; that the maximum they can apply on item B is 10 per cent and the maximum on item C is 15 per cent.
Freight Rates
Are all the rates to be reduced by 5 per cent so that item A will not be increased at all while items B and C will be subject to increases of 5 per cent and 10 per cent, or is there to be a ratable reduction; that is, a reduction of the same percentage applicable to each? For example, will all of these rates be reduced by 40 per cent so that the new reduced rates on items A, B and C would be respectively 3 per cent, 6 per cent and 9 per cent?
The number of items in the freight rate structure, as the minister knows, is very great and it seems logical to anticipate that a percentage reduction would be the simplest solution; in other words, a horizontal reduction of horizontal increases. This brings me to a point that will probably bring memories back to the minister. I remember so well when I was on the other side of the chamber how we were taunted about horizontal increases and how we were told that every time there was an increase in freight rates the effect of that increase was unjust and unfair because of the horizontal increases to which it applied. As I look at this subsidy I can see no remedy that will in any way attenuate the effect of horizontal increases.
I should like to bring to the attention of the committee a statement that was made by the acting Prime Minister on behalf of the government, the Minister of Public Works, in the absence of the Prime Minister, when the decision was taken by the government concerning this matter. Amongst other things, Madam Chairman, the hon. gentleman said:
It is however recognized by the government that there are serious inequities in the present freight rate structure which have both contributed to, and been aggravated by, the system of horizontal rate increases. The government has already indicated its intention to move toward a solution of these problems.
I submit that this subsidy is not in any way going to reduce the effect of these horizontal increases.
Perhaps at this point I should pause to commend and congratulate the hon. member for York-Humber who is now in the chair. I have been on the point of saying, "Mr. Chairman" once or twice, but on realizing who was in the chair I changed it to "Madam Chairman". This is a unique experience for me which I enjoy and I am sure I bespeak words on behalf of all hon. members, even my hon. friend to my left with whom I perhaps lost my patience a little too quickly this afternoon; on behalf of all of us I extend our congratulations.
I wish now to continue my argument. I am afraid the minister who made the statement to which I have just referred was not aware of the judgment; neither did he read

Freight Rates
the judgment of the board of transport commissioners. It runs right in the teeth of the statement he made. I do not think, sir,-

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Madam.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Thank you. I do not believe that horizontal increases can be disposed of in their serious implications on freight rates generally by this resolution. Let us see what the board of transport commissioners said about this question at page 14 of the judgment:
On every application for a general increase in freight rates the matter of a uniform percentage increase has been spoken to by the parties and considered by the board. The most recent expression of the board's views is contained in its 11 per cent judgment, and in the determination of this application for interim relief the board adopts those views, which are set forth as follows:
"The representations which have been made as to increased 'spreads' between long and short haul rates is by no means new. There are many critics who point up the undesirability of horizontal increases, particularly stressing the amounts in cents per one hundred pounds by which such 'spreads' increase, but it has not been shown in what way this feature can be avoided without either placing a higher rate burden on short haul traffic or reducing the earning power of the carriers by granting them rate levels too low to produce the revenue they should be entitled to seek for the service they provide".
Again, in the report of the royal commission which was established on transportation to deal with this matter of freight rates, there is a whole chapter by Mr. Justice Turgeon in which he deals with the effect of horizontal freight rates. On that occasion he made no recommendation in so far as a remedy for those rates was concerned. On the contrary, he stated that the matter was one for the railways and the board to determine.
The question naturally arises as to what the reduction would amount to in relation to the additional revenue which the increases are expected to yield. We know now that certain rates are being excepted; that competitive rates, international rates and import-export rates and the like are not covered in this resolution. But the minister said nothing about agreed charges. What about agreed charges? Are they covered in the subsidy? What about the piggy-back rates? Are they covered in the subsidy? When he rises to reply the minister should tell us because it is a matter of some importance to the house. What about coal and coke? Do they move under commodity rates, or are they excluded? If we assume that coal and coke, which always have been treated separately by the board, are outside the scope of the resolution, what is the amount of increase which would be subject to being affected by the proposed subsidy? To some extent the answer

is found on pages 29 and 30 of the judgment which gives the estimated results of this requested increase. From the traffic under the description "all other freight traffic" the C.N.R. expected a 19 per cent increase would yield $25.9 million, while the C.P.R. expected that on its traffic such an increase would yield $20.2 million, or a total of $46.1 million. The board, however, allowed an increase of only 17 per cent. If we assume that a 17 per cent increase would yield 17/19ths of the railways' estimate, we arrive at a figure of $41.2 million as the additional revenue that may be expected from a 17 per cent increase on this traffic.
However, as the minister stated, this resolution will apply in its implications not only to the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways but to other railways. There are other class 1 and class 2 railways to which application of this resolution will be made. Exact figures are not available to me of the dollar volume of this additional traffic, but we may safely assume that the aggregate increase for all carriers would be $41.2 million plus $4.8 million or a total of $46 million. A reduction for the whole of 1959 of $20 million applicable to that total would be equivalent to 43.5 per cent. But there is nothing in the resolution to indicate whether the reduction is to be made as a specific percentage of the increase, such as 43.5 per cent, or as a specific deduction from each rate; that is, 6 per cent or 7 per cent or 8 per cent to be deducted from the 17 per cent or whatever was the actual rate of increase, which would, in my view, be wholly impractical. However, the minister did say that this was the equivalent of a 7 per cent increase. I do not see how the minister is able to make that statement because I here say that the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways themselves are not able to say what increase they will receive in commodity rates, in normal rates, from the 17 per cent order, and if they are not able to say this, how then can the minister say that the reduction will be a 7 per cent decrease?
Some questions come to my mind along these lines. One of them has already been answered by the minister. I was going to ask him how long was this subsidy going to remain in force? He has answered by saying 12 months. What happens after the 12-month period? What will happen in the light of the present application which is now before the board for a 15 per cent increase in freight rates? The minister says that it will be held up pending the determination of the long term policy of the government. Suppose it takes two years before the long term policy of the government is determined. Does that

mean that meanwhile if there is an increase in cost, if there is an increase in the wages of the railway workers, the railways will not be entitled to receive the increase in freight rates because of this? The minister has certainly not cleared this up. I think that is one of the things he must do when he rises to reply because we know that if a royal commission is established, as has been indicated, it may take many months, it may take a year or two years before a recommendation is made upon the terms of reference which will have been given to it. Does this mean that in the meantime those workers who may be entitled to increased wages because of the increased costs will be held up in their demands, or does it mean that the minister will then come along with another such resolution in which he will increase the $20 million by another amount which will look after those increased wages? If that is so, then this is in effect a way a subsidizing of wages.
Another question which arises is the following. We have observed that not all competitive rates will be increased to the full extent authorized by the board. Some of this traffic will stand only a smaller increase, perhaps 10 per cent instead of 17 per cent. In the same way some normal rated traffic may be able to stand an increase of 10 per cent. Let us suppose that such is the case. Is it the government's intention that the traffic moving under the competitive rate shall pay the full increase of 10 per cent, because in the resolution traffic moving under competitive rates is expressly excluded, but the traffic moving under normal rates shall pay only a part of the increase of 10 per cent? Would this not lead in some instances to a further revision of the rates, so that the shipper would qualify for the lower rate, with the government making good the resulting deficiency?
But apart from these questions which arise from an examination of how the proposed subsidy will work out and how it is to be applied, there is a much more important question than that. What problem is solved by this subsidy? Does it solve any problem or is it not merely a complicating factor? Does not the granting of this subsidy merely postpone this very serious and grave issue which is before the government? Does not the granting of this subsidy merely in effect do what the government ought to have done many months ago when the serious railway problem came before it for attention?
So, sir, I have no hesitation in declaring to the house that this resolution is nothing but a stop-gap arrangement. It is nothing more than the kind of solution that the government has applied to all problems. It
Freight Rates
allows all major problems to develop to a state of crisis before it acts and then it acts by writing out another cheque.
The government has known that it would have to deal with this problem since November of 1957 when the unions representing the non-operating employees of the railways served demands for increased wages, improved fringe benefits and changes in working rules. It may not have known with certainty what amount of money would be ultimately involved when these demands were finally dealt with but the government did know after the award of the conciliation board in September, 1958 how much money would have to be found. However, in characteristic fashion it waited until the last minute before it came to a decision that can only be regarded at best as an interim. I strongly believe that the interim measure will make the problem more difficult to solve and will give rise to innumerable smaller problems.
What is the government's long term policy? I think the minister owes it to the committee to tell us what the government's long term policy is. After all, parliament is being asked to vote a subsidy of $20 million and then, when it suits their convenience, the government will announce their long term policy either in the form of an investigation as I indicated last night or a royal commission. I do not think it is fair to parliament any more than it is to the people of Canada to ask for the passage of this measure without knowing what the intention of the government is. Is it intended to have an investigation into the complex freight rate structure of the country? Is it intended that there shall be a royal commission to consider the whole railway transportation problem of Canada? I believe that these things should be known before the passage of this resolution is approved.
I think we should also be told, as I said earlier, on what basis the $20 million is to be handed out. What will happen to the freight rate structure as a result of the application of the $20 million? All the minister said was that certain rates were excluded but that is not clear enough. I think that those who are particularly interested, the provinces and the railways, will want to know how this formula is to be applied. When the railways themselves have some difficulty even today in arriving at the amount of money which will be derived from the 17 per cent increase, it becomes all the more difficult to ascertain how this formula is to be applied. The minister knows that the railways are having difficulties today in increasing their rates in the light of the 17 per cent judgment. The ceilings go up but the amounts they

Freight Rates
are able to charge for traffic is uncertain and very often freight will not move on the increased rate. If the railways are having difficulties in the application of the 17 per cent increase, then a fortiori there will be difficulty unless there is a clear formula in the application of the $20 million reduction.
I think the minister is oversimplifying the situation. I think the minister believes that it is an easy formula and easy to work out. I can tell the minister that when it came to providing a formula for the $7 million bridge subsidy a tremendous amount of thinking went into the matter and the situation then, I submit with deference, was not nearly as serious as it is now. The committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines spent many hours, indeed many days, in trying to iron out a formula. It heard many representations and arrived at a formula on the basis of the trackage, the mileage, and the maintenance of that trackage over the bridge.
How is the formula going to be applied here? There is nothing indicative of that in anything that has been said by the minister so far. So I say that this matter certainly cannot be dealt with on an interim basis but must be carefully studied. The previous administration, which had a great deal of experience in this regard, proceeded by a measure which directed the board of transport commissioners to equalize freight rates and by the appointment of a royal commission to study the whole railway problem. Is the government going to do the same thing? I think the minister should tell us.
While I am on that subject, I should like to say that all of the recommendations made by the royal commission on transportation with regard to freight rates were put into effect by the former government. The minister will recall that when he sat on this side of the house we were condemned by the minister and his friends because of what we were doing at the time. The board of transport commissioners was condemned. It was said that the board of transport commissioners was useless, that its members were not performing their job. As a matter of fact, at one stage there was a motion to reduce the estimates of the board of transport commissioners to $1. That was the extent of the contribution made by some hon. members on the other side of the house at that time, but now when they are in office not only do they not dismiss the members of the board of transport commissioners but they do exactly what was done by their predecessors. They renew the appointments of certain members of the board.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: I just have one sentence before I conclude. In my opinion this measure will not solve the difficult railway and railway freight problem. We on this side of the house are extremely anxious to see the formula which will be applied and under which the board of transport commissioners will operate in distributing the subsidy of $20 million. I hope the minister will be able to let us see the bill after the passage of the resolution so that we can study all its implications.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Before the hon. member speaks, may I answer the questions put to me?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
No. It is the custom of the house to hear a representative from each of the parties. I know the Minister of Transport is most anxious to follow our normal procedure because he is one who takes a great interest in the rules of the house and is always most co-operative on that score. This announcement by the Minister of Transport demonstrates that the government has broken another solemn commitment to the Canadian people, namely to prevent further increases in discriminatory freight rates. The policy of the Conservative party has been made clear in the past. The Prime Minister has made it clear. The Minister of Transport himself has spoken very often on this and other questions. The Prime Minister, in Drumheller, Alberta, on May 18, 1957, had this to say, according to press reports:
At Drumheller he said there should be equalization of rail rates in Canada "within reasonable limits" to give a shot in the arm to agriculture and industry on the prairies.
The Canadian Press report says:
On freight rates, he said, that a rate pattern discriminatory to the west has been made worse by recent increases. This had struck "an almost paralyzing blow" to industrial development in the west.
In the Globe and Mail, we find this report:
He said a Conservative government would equalize freight rates as far as possible to help both agriculture and industry on the prairies compete with the rest of Canada.
Before the last general election when the board of transport commissioners had granted a 3.6 per cent increase and the government did not have this tremendous majority, they acted forthrightly, they acted with courage. They said to the board of transport commissioners that this increase would not be allowed. However, in this instance, the government not only failed to prevent an increase in freight rates but through this legislation which is forecast by the resolution and in the words of the minister they are allowing a net increase of 10 per cent even after this $20 million subsidy becomes effective.

We have now had in this country since the end of the war, a long series of increases in freight rates. The total increase to date amounts to 157 per cent. This imposes a great burden upon the remote areas of Canada, particularly the prairie provinces, British Columbia and the maritimes. Even with this legislation, this government is allowing the same practices and the same conditions to prevail as were allowed under the previous administration. We think the government should have taken the same position they took with regard to the 3.6 per cent, namely to have disallowed the 17 per cent. The government was requested to disallow the increase by eight provinces. Seldom on public matters do the provinces of this country speak with the type of unity with which they speak with regard to freight rates. Only two provinces did not join with the others in protesting increases in freight rates. I think the provincial governments of Ontario and Quebec make a mistake in not protesting increases in freight rates. I believe this is particularly true because these rates affect the more remote regions of these provinces.
The Ontario government is apparently quite ready to allow horizontal increases in freight rates to discriminate against the whole of the northern sections of Ontario. I feel the premier of Ontario has been derelict in his duty in not joining with the other eight provinces that have protested the increases in freight rates. There are a number of reasons why I feel the premier of Ontario should join with the other provinces in this regard. The main reason, of course, the economic reason, is that an increase in freight rates damages the economy of northern and northwestern Ontario. The premier of Ontario should show concern when that large section of the province is adversely affected by the actions of this government.
There is another reason why I feel the premier of Ontario should join with the other provinces and that is that perhaps he, above all others, may have some influence on this government. I would hope that in the future he would correct this very serious error and mistake. The board of transport commissioners over the years has allowed a great many increases in freight rates. I have in my hand a list of the various increases in freight rates which have been allowed since the end of the war. The number of increases, although some of them were parts of subsequent total increases, amounts to seven since the end of the war.
In assessing the need for an increase in freight rates, the board has taken the financial position of the Canadian Pacific as a yardstick, that is the net profit position. There
Freight Rates
has been a consistent and continuing complaint from the eight provinces that on this basis of assessing the freight rate requirements of this country the board of transport commissioners has been in very serious error. The board has failed to take into account the fact that the Canadian Pacific has set aside very large depletion and depreciation reserves which, in the opinion of the eight provinces, are excessive and should not be allowed. The Canadian Pacific is a mammoth organization which operates steamships and hotels and owns the controlling interest in Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, owns very large tracts of lands and holds the mineral rights on those tracts of land.
A few years ago the Canadian Pacific was showing a substantial profit because of oil revenues and revenues from its mineral rights on the land it holds, so they transferred the land from their general account to a separate account in order to make the Canadian Pacific balance sheet show a smaller profit. The board of transport commissioners by its actions in the past has shown that it is incapable of solving the problem of discriminatory freight rates in this country. We require today, I believe, a firm announcement by the government that there shall be no further horizontal increases in freight rates. The minister has said there will be no increases for a certain period of time until certain studies are made. I do not believe that is an adequate guarantee. We should have a forthright statement from the government that they will not allow further increases in freight rates in this country.
The railway must have sufficient revenue to operate. The workers who are employed by the railway companies should have a wage level in keeping with the workers in comparable occupations in this country. However, there is no reason, in our opinion, why the board should take the Canadian Pacific as the yardstick and grant increases as it has done in the past. There should be no automatic increase in freight rates because of an increase in costs, no matter what those costs may be. In the early years of confederation, it was decided under the national policy that it was necessary to the preservation of Canada as a nation to have a transcontinental railway, and subsequently to have further transcontinental railways.
It was recognized that the railroad was in some instances built through areas that were not productive, when the normal course of the railway might have been to go south of the great lakes through the United States; and some recognition was given to that consideration by the payment of a $7 million subsidy for the so-called bridge. In the opinion of the C.C.F. it is time that we adopted

Freight Rates
a national transportation policy. We believe that the government should set up a national transportation authority that would have jurisdiction over all transportation matters coming under the federal government and that its declared policy should be to equalize freight rates and to make them apply equitably in all parts of Canada.
The government is going to have to decide whether or not it will continue the present rule, namely to grant freight rate increases so that the C.P.R. will show extremely large profits, or whether it will take into account the legitimate economic interests of the maritime provinces, western Canada and the remoter sections of the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec.
From the Minister of Transport we have had so far a brief statement. In introducing a measure such as this one which entails the expenditure of $20 million, I would have thought that the minister in charge of it would have given the house the benefit of a comprehensive review of this whole question. The minister has not done that. Although the minister's major statement to the house was relatively short, I doubt that it contained as much pertinent information as the statements he made during the speech delivered last night by the hon. member for Laurier. We seem to have the government policy coming out by dribs and drabs. The Minister of Transport, interrupting the hon. member for Laurier, gave us some important information. He said this as reported at page 2208 of Hansard:
In the meantime the government does not propose to permit any further general increases in railway freight rates.
It would be interesting to know what period this statement covers. Does the government during this parliament intend to prevent further increases in freight rates or does the government merely intend to prevent further increases in freight rates during the next 12 months? What is the government's policy with respect to further increases in freight rates?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question at this point? It is only intended for explanatory purposes and is not antagonistic.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Did I understand the hon. member to say that his group favoured the fixation of the present rates and that no permit ever be granted to raise the rates and at the same time to assure that the railways would continue to operate services of benefit to Canadians and pay what we all hope would be decent living wages to railway

employees? I wonder what policy he had in mind. How can he reconcile these two objectives? How can you procure from the railroads this type of service and salaries or wages without providing some method for them to recoup their income?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Of course there must be some method. I made the statement-and I think the hon. member was able to grasp it-that there should be no further horizontal freight rate increases in this country, and that there should be no further increases in commodity rates in this country. If it is necessary-and it may well be-from time to time to provide additional revenues to the railways because of increased costs, the necessity of providing additional services or improved services, then those additional costs should come from the national treasury. That is not a new statement. That is not something that is new today. The province of Saskatchewan argued this matter before the board of transport commissioners long before the establishment of the Turgeon royal commission which subsequently reported on February 29, 1951. It is interesting to know that that particular policy which the Saskatchewan government originated and initiated is getting greater and greater support from provincial governments across this country.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit one further question?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Is the hon. member suggesting that as a form of policy his group would support the endowing of a private corporate carrier, namely the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, out of the national treasury in such circumstances as he sets forth?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
We do it all the time. This government is doing it now. The hon. member has been asking me questions. I think I have the right to answer his questions. The government is doing it now with $20 million. When the question is put to the house I am certain it will receive a unanimous vote. But we also say that when the government is endowing the C.P.R. with a large part of the $20 million, an entirely different yardstick should be taken in the setting of freight rates. We say that the C.P.R. has been given larger freight rates than are necessary had the board of transport commissioners taken into account the total financial position of this mammoth and sprawling octopus, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, instead of taking into account merely the freight and railway operations of the company. The C.P.R. is in a wonderful position. The air

transport board, with the government's approval, has given C.P.A.L., a C.P.R. subsidiary a chance to extend their facilities to haul passengers on transcontinental operations. The C.P.R. is in the trucking business in an extensive way. This company is in competition with itself. The more successful the C.P.R. trucking firms become, the higher the freight rates that must be paid by my hon. friend's constituents and the people of the maritime provinces and by the people who live in the western provinces. We say that it is time for a national transportation policy that would prevent further discrimination and further burdens upon the remote areas of this country. Of course that has been the declared policy of the Prime Minister since 1940. But he has made a complete reversal since he has become Prime Minister. Even with the $20 million subsidy the government is allowing a further increase in discriminatory freight rates.
We would be greatly interested in knowing whether we are to have another royal commission to look into the freight rate question. We had the Turgeon royal commission which presented a comprehensive and detailed report. The hon. member for Laurier says that all of the recommendations dealing with equalization have now been implemented. Yet freight rates are more unequal in this country than they were when the report was given to this house. As the years go by, under the corrective policy of the former administration, and under the new freight rate policy in revision, freight rates become higher, discrimination increases, and the burden on the remote sections of this country goes up. We are interested to know whether there is to be another royal commission. The member for Laurier last night said this:
When I interrupted the minister I gathered from him that it would follow in due course that a statement would be made about the appointment of a royal commission. I did not hear that statement made but I take it that in the course of the debate at a later stage it is the intention of the minister to make that kind of announcement and to state also the terms of reference of the royal commission.
The minister replied as follows:
I might answer the hon. member for Laurier on that point now, Mr. Chairman. A much larger, long term inquiry is under very active consideration by the government at the present time and I expect that in the very near future the Prime Minister will be making the kind of announcement to which the hon. member has referred.
I ask, is that a royal commission? How can the Prime Minister make the announcement at a later date when the Minister of Transport leaks it to the house in making the announcement that he made last night in advance of the Prime Minister?
Freight Rates
I notice that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is in his seat. There has been a great deal of speculation as to what went on in the cabinet circles last fall when they were considering the 17 per cent increase in freight rates and the judgment which had been made by the board of transport commissioners. I have in my hand the Motor Carrier for February, 1959, which is a trade publication for truck and bus operators in Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. It has a very interesting paragraph on page 6 which is headed "Secret Sessions" and reads as follows:
Behind closed cabinet doors in the east block Diefenbakermen-
Not Conservatives, note; "Diefenbakermen"-
-Gordon Churchill (Manitoba) and Alvin Hamilton (Saskatchewan), had been fighting for the same remedy but opposed by finance minister Donald Fleming, generally regarded as the mouthpiece of the powerful Tory "eastern group" of finance and investment houses.
There was a tremendous skirmish in the cabinet last fall, according to this report.
Churchill, supported in spirit at least by Manitoba Prime Minister Duff Roblin-
That is about all the support you would get, I guess, from a Tory colleague, "in spirit"-
-threatened to resign and then, as all good politicians and party stalwarts must do, subsequently denied such action.
Out of the stormy sessions came the decision to set up a special cabinet study committee under the chairmanship of Hon, A. J. Brooks.
We would like to know if this special cabinet committee has been established. We would appreciate any comments from the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to the important role he played in pressuring his colleagues to act at least in this meager way. But in the light of those statements, I think the statement made by the hon. Minister of Transport last night takes on a great significance when he seemed to fence in his own Prime Minister by announcing to the house the statement which the Prime Minister would make at a later date. People of Canada who are bearing these tremendous burdens of freight rates are fed up to the teeth with royal commissions. We have had royal commissions into freight rates time and time again. We have had royal commissions in other fields. This is becoming a government by royal commission.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: What about your provincial government in Saskatchewan?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: The provincial government in Saskatchewan is doing very well.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
You have had royal commissions, though.

Freight Rates

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
We have had royal commissions, as the hon. minister of northern affairs has said, in fields where no other provincial government has acted; so that Saskatchewan has the distinction of having the first reports in this field. But this government says, following the other administration: Me too. This is a hot potato. We are obviously not fulfilling our election promises; we are repudiating them, so we will set up a royal commission. We can hide behind a royal commission for a year or so. When the royal commission brings in its report, we can say it supersedes our definite election promises to the people of this country.
Those Canadians who live in the maritimes and in western Canada, the remote areas of Ontario and Quebec, say that this government has failed to fulfil its election promise to the people of Canada to prevent further increases in discriminatory freight rates. All this legislation does at best is to reduce the very serious effect of this last increase in freight rates. What this government is doing by this legislation is saying, "We shall allow freight rates in this country to be a somewhat greater burden on freight users than the very high freight rates allowed by the previous administration, about which we complained so bitterly." This is a bits-and-pieces government. This government has no policy in this field except to follow the pattern of the previous administration in hiding behind royal commissions, adding discriminatory freight rates to discriminatory freight rates, and failing to enunciate a national transportation policy that would provide equitable freight rates to all parts of this nation.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution moved last evening by the Minister of Transport concerns very seriously every province of Canada and particularly the Atlantic provinces. This resolution deals with a measure which will result in a reduction of certain class and commodity freight rates other than competitive rates. It also provides for payments to reimburse carriers for the resulting reduction of their revenues up to an aggregate amount of $20 million. The passing of such a measure will undoubtedly reduce substantially the 17 per cent increase which was authorized by the board of transport commissioners' order of November 17, 1958. In fact, it is calculated that the 17 per cent increase authorized by that order will be reduced to approximately 11 per cent, and even to 10 per cent, according to the minister's figures of last evening following the application of the measure now to be introduced.
I would like to deal at this time with the freight rate structure as it applies particularly to the Atlantic provinces. Increases in our

Canadian freight rate structure have been numerous and quite substantial, particularly in the postwar period. Every Canadian citizen will recognize the handicap which the Atlantic provinces have to contend with due to difficulties of transportation, partially accounted for by our geographical position with regard to the more heavily populated sections of Canada. In fact, owing to economic, geographic and other disadvantages, the Atlantic provinces are adversely affected by transportation difficulties and are liable to suffer more from any increases which affect tariffs of tolls and rates than any other area of the country. The distance from and the cost of transportation to the great continental market centres has always been a serious handicap to maritime producers. Freight subventions extended under the Maritime Freight Rates Act have tended to offset in part only the disadvantages which affected development of our industries in the maritimes. This transportation problem has in fact been a basic part of the plan for confederation. The railway rate structure determines the distribution of railway costs between several regions and also determines to what degree different industrial and regional groups contribute to the payment of such costs.
The advantage of the Maritime Freight Rates Act enacted in 1927 by a Liberal administration, partially offsetting the disadvantage of maritime producers in relation to the central Canada market, were gradually nullified by further reductions in freight rates made by the railways themselves in central Canada to meet truck competition. It is true that a great deal has been done in recent years to offset the higher cost of marketing the products of the producers of the Atlantic region caused by the long distances between that region and markets in central Canada. This was followed by improved means of communication within the Atlantic region itself. It was agreed, as announced in March of 1957, that a thorough and comprehensive examination of the entire transportation situation in the maritime provinces should be undertaken to determine the possibility of introducing changes which could contribute to the economic welfare of this region.
The Minister of Finance then expressed the government's intention to launch an immediate review of the maritime transportation problem in general in order to put forward as soon as possible proposals to improve the transportation system generally. As a temporary measure to meet the special disadvantages offered by horizontal increases in freight rates, increases which we know have fallen more heavily on outbound traffic from the maritimes, an increase in the subventions paid under the Maritime Freight Rates Act

was authorized in 1957, extending such subventions from the level of 20 per cent to the present level of 30 per cent.
When the 1958 estimates for the Department of Transport were discussed in the house the Minister of Transport was asked by the hon. member for Laurier if the study of the interdepartmental committee on maritime transportation had been completed and if a report on the matter could be expected at an early date. The minister's reply will be found on page 4357 of Hansard for August 30, 1958. I quote:
This whole question is under intensive study at the present time, and we expect to have a report on it by the end of the year.
The end of the year has passed and we are still waiting. The freight rate boosts have moved so fast in the last decade, as was mentioned today, that we have had seven increases in the past eight years. They have increased by 154 per cent and a further request for another 12 to 15 per cent increase is now before the board of transport commissioners. The result of these increases has been a reduction in the value of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. We were pleased to hear from the minister his statement that no further increases are contemplated for the next 12 months. The reductions asked for in the measure to be introduced by the government and presently under debate will be of extremely limited advantage to the Atlantic provinces.
The terms of confederation clearly established that the maritimes should have cheap access to the markets of central Canada. The present Maritime Freight Rates Act as it now applies barely cushions the full impact of the climbing freight rates over the last 10 or 12 years. The present railway charges have a tendency to accentuate the decline of manufacturing in the Atlantic provinces and in other outlying parts of Canada. This policy is clearly reflected by the tendency of our Canadian industries to concentrate their operations right in the middle of the market or at the nearest possible distribution point.
The people of the maritimes have become more and more aware that what is needed today is the bold, comprehensive and coordinated approach to our transportation problem which was so clearly indicated in the Gordon commission report. The narrowing of such differences and disadvantages by effective changes in the horizontal per ton mile policy of rate increases will substantially help the maritimes to improve the present climate for industrial development. The plea of the maritimes is based on a confederation commitment which involves the importance of our access to central Canadian markets
Freight Rates
which access is deteriorating due mainly to the increased cost of transportation together with the contraction of foreign markets particularly as these questions affect our lumber industry.
I should like to quote one paragraph of the report of the Turgeon commission which dealt with transportation. At page 27 in the third paragraph outlining alleged disadvantages, we read:
The maritime provinces state that when compared to central Canada their economy is found to be deteriorating and that this trend is influenced by the increased cost of transportation to central Canada and by the contraction of foreign markets; for example the loss of markets for apples, lumber and pit props in the United Kingdom, and potatoes in the United States.
The case of the maritimes may be summarized: At confederation they were promised access to the central Canadian market. Today, in view of the deterioration in foreign trade, particularly because of monetary and commercial restrictions, access to the central Canadian market has become more important than ever. Isolation of the maritimes from the central Canadian area as a result of distance and of increased freight charges is one of the central themes put forward in their case. A witness for the transportation commission of the maritime board of trade, when asked whether or not the maritimes were willing to accept their disadvantages provided they retained their advantages, replied:
"The national background in connection with our intercolonial railway was to afford persons and industries to get into the markets of central Canada. That is the basic principle."
The Maritime Freight Rates Act is regarded as the instrument intended to facilitate access to the central Canadian markets. It was suggested by the same witness that this instrument is losing its effectiveness:
"The general tenor of the evidence of the maritime approach ... is that the changes which have taken place since the Maritime Freight Rates Act became effective in 1927 are having the effect of enhancing the difficulty of maritime producers in reaching the highly competitive markets of central Canada in competition with industries located closer to the markets."
The report of this royal commission is perhaps the best document ever prepared on the subject of freight rate problems in the maritimes and other sections of Canada affected by transportation difficulties. Maritime shippers claimed, and rightly so, that recent changes have decreased the advantages which the rates established under the act of 1927 intended to confer on the maritimes. I may not want to go as far as to disapprove of the statutory Crowsnest pass agreement but nevertheless the rest of Canada must be made aware-and this applies particularly to the prairie provinces-that the board of transport commissioners are not now in a position to grant rates which are just and reasonable to the lumber industries because of inequities in the rate structure which are beyond the board's power. This matter was dealt with

Freight Rates
thoroughly in the submission of the Canadian lumbermen's association to the cabinet committee on freight rates on January 9 of this year. Without disapproving of the Crowsnest pass agreement, I would suggest however that its application should motivate the government to give further consideration to the added burden which is automatically thrown on other traffic, including lumber.
The Canadian lumbermen's association is rightly concerned about the effect of increased freight rates on lumber which is called upon to bear such a proportion of each mileage rate increase when applied to our eastern Canadian lumber industry.
I am not surprised to see the New Brunswick sawn lumber production decrease from a total of 281 million board feet in 1956 to 244 million in 1957 and to 198 million in 1958, a reduction of approximately 30 per cent in the period of the last three years. I am not surprised also that our lumber dealers are under the impression that the lumber rates are being called upon more and more to subsidize the statutory grain rates. This leads me to remind the government of the events leading to confederation in 1867, and of the responsibilities deriving from this union of the provinces. There must be, however, ways and means of adjusting existing differences without interfering with the present arrangement for the transportation of grain to ports of exit. It must be recognized, however, that lumber provides earnings in excess of the national average, and such finished commodities as veneer and plywood are far beyond the national average rate. Such anomalies should not be allowed in our national transportation system, and adequate measures should be found to correct these irregularities by the application of a long range plan formulated to give equal opportunity and equal justice to all concerned.
In a formal statement issued by the government, following the acceptance of a new freight rate increase in November of last year, it was admitted that there are serious inequities in the present freight rate structure which have both contributed to and been aggravated by the system of horizontal rate increases. The government informed the country that a study was being undertaken at once to work out measures to relieve the inequities in the freight rate structure, including any that may be aggravated by the last increase of 17 per cent. It was made clear that the intention of the government was to provide both an immediate alleviation of discrimination where it exists and a long term solution to the broader problems. Recent events, such as the last increase mentioned, which has been followed by a new demand for a further increase of 14 to 15 
per cent will definitely make it difficult for the government to carry on with its "hold-the-line" policy of fighting the wage-price spiral and inflation which we are facing today. Again I want to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that we were pleased to learn from the minister last evening that it is the intention of the government not to allow any further increase, at least for a limited period.
It is true that the approval of the measure to be followed by the present resolution will reduce by approximately one-third the additional burden of the latest freight rate increase. It is also true that the major share of this increase is being paid by the western and the Atlantic provinces, and such boosts place unfair burdens on Canada's outlying regions. Horizontal increases, when applied on a uniform percentage basis, destroy the advantages which the Maritime Freight Rates Act was designed to give to our area. This measure introduced by the government at the present time will do very little to alleviate this situation.
We all remember that one of the main pledges of the Atlantic resolutions which, as I have stated before in this house, is very familiar to government members, was to bring the maritimes a better transportation deal. It has been made clear that 75 per cent of this increase will fall on classes of rates which provide the railways with only 32 per cent of their revenues. In other words, roughly one-third of the railway traffic is being asked today to pay about three-quarters of the revenue which the railways expect to derive from the last rate boost. We in the Atlantic provinces are on the receiving end of this iniquitous additional burden and the pledge of the Atlantic resolutions must be implemented without delay to protect the vital interests of the Atlantic provinces in this matter of transportation.
It has been stated that the role of the railways was to serve the Atlantic interests without prejudicing particular industries and areas. The application of a similar policy resulted in the implementation of the Maritime Freight Rates Act in 1927, but events of the last 10 or 12 years clearly show that the advantages of such an act are being scuttled under the series of rate increases which have reached over 106 per cent since 1949. We want to make it clear that the outlying regions of the country cannot be expected to bear the heaviest share of the burden in serving the national interest, and this applies also to the fight against the present trend of inflation, which is a serious menace to the economy of the country.
We are asking the government for full compensation for the inequalities imposed upon us, and we insist on legislation which

will provide a formula to protect us from the ill effects of future rate increases which are expected to follow.
While we will support the present legislation we reserve the right, however, to regard it as a temporary measure only, which will alleviate in part the discrimination in Canada's freight rate structure. It is only a half way measure which does not provide the full protection promised in the Atlantic resolutions, and is far from reaching this new deal which would give our products easy access to the markets of Canada.
