In 1953, a combine cost $5,750 while in 1959 the cost is $9,800, an increase of $4,000. Much of the increase reflects increased labour costs as well as increased freight costs. That is just one example and I am going to give a few more. That is why this legislation will be welcomed by the farmers of the province of Alberta.
There is one thing that is overlooked by the hon. member for Assiniboia when he talks about freight rates and this matter is sometimes misunderstood in western Canada. The Crowsnest pass rates have been in existence since 1897 and apply to the shipment of various grains. We have been assured by the Prime Minister and the government that they will remain in existence. I am certain that the farmers of my constituency and elsewhere in the province of Alberta welcome that.
I should like to give a few more examples of increased costs, and increased costs are the reason why if some western farmer were here this afternoon and could speak instead of myself he would support the resolution. Over a period of five years the price of a self-propelled swather, for example, has increased by $200. Tractor prices have increased by $1,700. Prices of disc hauls have gone up $710, and so on. I could give a whole list of farm machinery to show that costs have doubled since 1953.
Much of the increase has been due to increased labour costs. When I listen to the hon. member for Assiniboia, who comes from the same province in which I was raised, I often wonder why he does not tell the full story. We in western Canada know that the 17 per cent increase in freight rates came about because the men of the railways asked for an increase in wages. Now the government is acting to cut the increase to 10 per cent with the result that the men on the railways have got their increase and the farmers of western Canada have the advantage of the $20 million provided in the resolution. That seems to be the whole story.
When the members of the C.C.F. speak either in the province of Saskatchewan or

in this house I always feel that they only tell half the story and leave the other half untold. That is what prompted me to say a few words on behalf of the province of Alberta. Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to learn that the C.C.F. has influence in rural Alberta. That is the finest news I have heard in the house for some days. I wish to endorse the plea that a national transportation policy be established. We are being asked today to provide the railroads of Canada with an amount of $20 million. There are many Canadians who look a bit askance each time the parliament of Canada is asked for what amounts to a handout or subsidy to any one enterprise. Therefore when we are asked to vote $20 million to the railroads of Canada it causes us to consider the terms under which the subsidy will be paid.
I notice that the resolution contains one term, namely that the subsidy will be paid if there is a reduction in certain rates. All the speeches thus far have tended to deal only with the condition of rates. I can defend the policy of the government in handing to the railway companies a fixed sum of money if the railways are offering services to the Canadian public that are not in themselves of a profit-making nature, and I believe that is the main argument underlying the resolution. The people of the far eastern and western provinces are to be given some relief and the taxpayers generally are being asked to share with them the heavy burden of moving goods to and from central Canada.
I think that the resolution will receive the unanimous support of members of the house. However, I should like to see the terms imposed on the railroads take in a few other factors as well. I believe that all Canadians, so far as is reasonably possible, should have available to them the services of Canadian railways. What I have in mind at this time may involve something that would not mean
[Mr. Woolliams.l
a great net return to the railroad companies. However, in travelling to Toronto from western Ontario recently on the C.P.R. line I was rather impressed by something I observed. The train came to a stop and we were informed that we had arrived at West Toronto. Some miles beyond the train again came to a stop and we were told we had arrived at the suburb station of Parkdale. I looked out the window and saw the C.P.R. station. Then I looked out another window and saw the C.N.R. station. In other words, Parkdale a suburb of Toronto, has two railway stations. Several miles farther on the train finally arrived at the union station.
The point I want to make is that if the people of Canada are going to be asked to subsidize the railroads then as many of them as possible should be given service by the railroad. In metropolitan Toronto there is a reasonable number of railroad stations to serve the suburban areas and the same situation prevails in the suburbs of Montreal. However, hitherto the railroad companies have refused to extend the same service to the suburbs of other metropolitan areas of Canada. I fail to understand why, for example, the municipality of Burnaby from which I come, with a population of 100,000, should continually be denied the service of a railway station. Possibly one reason why the people of Burnaby do not use the railways more than they do is that they always have to go to the heart of the city of Vancouver if they want to do any business with the railways. If the people of Burnaby are going to be taxed in order to provide this subsidy, then I believe that the railway companies should give some consideration to providing our people with as many railway facilities as can be reasonably provided.
I have noted that we are being asked for a subsidy for the operation of railroads and I assume that most of the major railway companies in Canada will be involved. We have the Canadian National railways, Canadian Pacific railway, the Pacific Great Eastern railway, the Northern Alberta railway, and I do not know exactly how many other companies that are going to be involved in this subsidy.
If we are speaking of subsidies, then the people of British Columbia have a claim against the federal treasury. We hope that before the government goes too far in subsidizing the operations of railroads they will remember that they have not yet paid us the customary railroad building subsidy for the extension of the Pacific Great Eastern from Prince George into the Peace river block. If we are speaking of subsidies, let us put first things first, and let us pay off this obligation

which is owing to British Columbia for the building of that railroad extension.
One of the services that we expect the railroad companies to supply to the Canadian people, and for which we are willing to allow subsidies, is what we often call the unprofitable branch line services. We contend, and I think parliament has accepted over the years, that many areas of Canada must be served by railroads, whether or not such service means a net return to the company. It is for that purpose that in the past much money has been voted to the railroads by this house and likely will again in the years to come.
I am not making particular reference at this time to the fairly well populated sections of Alberta that are going to be asked to share in the cost of this subsidy. However, there is a section of Alberta in which the people have been waiting for the services of a railroad for 40 years or more. I regretted very much the other evening that the members from northern Alberta could not seem to make up their minds as to where the proposed new railroad ought to be built. I have no hesitation at all in advocating that this railroad be built up in a northwesterly direction to connect with the Pacific Great Eastern. This would supply much needed rail service to the thousands of people living in the farm communities north of Grimshaw, Alberta.
I do not want to become involved in the argument as to whether the extension should go from Pine Point to Grimshaw or Pine Point to Dawson. This is a matter for others to decide. However, if the farmers around Fort Vermilion, who will have to pay for this subsidy, had this railroad extension they would receive over 30 cents more for each bushel of wheat they had to sell. I do not see why the government should even contemplate the building of a railroad in a southeasterly direction, mostly over rock, when there is southwest of the Great Slave lake, old, settled communities that have waited for so very long for the fulfilment of an obligation assumed by those who encouraged them to settle there many years ago.
I know the minister is anxious to reply, and I have only one other non-profitable service to list. I am going to be very brief. I think all members of this committee would much more gladly allow this subsidy to be paid to the railroad companies of Canada if these companies gave a fair deal to the older, retired pensioners. In this connection, I would specifically refer to the Canadian Pacific railway which, since 1947, has allowed a 45 per cent increase in the pensions of those of its employees who worked and are retired in the United States. who were retired prior to 1953, and who had worked and lived in Canada, have never received any increase at all. It is shameful that so many of these people have to eke out their last days on pensions of $35 and $40 a month.

Before I say anything on that matter I should like to tell him and the other members of the committee that this plan for alleviating the burden of freight rates, as we are doing, was not worked out in a casual manner whatsoever. A great deal of time and thought were put on it. It is an extremely difficult problem. It was worked on during many meetings by a committee composed of cabinet ministers and officials.
The plan which has been arrived at has the full concurrence of and was worked out by the chief commissioner of the board of transport commissioners and his experts. I have great pleasure in assuring the hon. member for Laurier that I have been assured and the committee was assured that this is a workable plan. Also one of the reasons for referring this bill to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines is this. If there are technical questions having to do with freight rates and their operation,

that committee will afford to all hon. members an ideal opportunity to question officials on the more technical aspects of this bill and how it will operate. However, I think I can generally answer the questions put to me by the hon. member for Laurier by going back over a few of the things I said in my opening statement. With regard to how this formula will be applied, which was the question asked by the hon. member, 1 said this as reported at page 2207 of Hansard:
As an interim measure designed to alleviate the burden of the authorized increase in rates, the proposed legislation provides for a subsidy of $20 million over a 12-month period, to be paid to the companies that are subject to the board's order No. 96300 as reimbursement for such reductions in rates as they may be directed to make pursuant to this legislation. The companies that are subject to order No. 96300, and thereby come within the scope of this legislation, are principally the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and its leased lines, and a number of smaller railway companies which are member lines of the railway association of Canada; and the water carriers who participate in joint water-rail, and rail-water-rail routes, that is the Canada Steamship Lines, Northwest Steamship Company and Canadian Pacific Great Lakes Steamships-
The legislation provides that the board shall require the companies to reduce their class and commodity rates by such amounts as to effect a reduction in their revenues obtained from this traffic by $20 million during a 12-month period. The exact reduction in rates which will thereby result is a matter which will depend upon traffic volume and not one which the government, by legislation, could fix in advance. I may say, however, that on the basis of the present volume and pattern of traffic it has been estimated that the application of the $20 million subsidy on the basis which I have outlined will permit a reduction of some seven percentage points, thereby making the authorized increase approximately 10 per cent in lieu of 17 per cent.
That is the general pattern of how the reduction will be made. As far as the technical details are concerned, the chief commissioner of the board of transport commissioners has assured me that there will be no problem arising there, and that it could be done with relative ease. If there are other technical questions which the hon. member for Laurier would like to ask with regard to how this will be done, I would suggest that those questions will most easily be answered when the committee meets.

speechtext: Could I say this, Mr. Chairman? If British Columbia is suffering the most, then British Columbia will get the most.

speechtext: I will be very happy to accept what the minister has said, if he would just explain how British Columbia will benefit most under the proposition now before us. I remember very well only a few years ago a former member sitting on the same side of the house, a Liberal, by the name of McGeer, put up a fight on behalf of freight rates as far as British Columbia was concerned. He was the first man who found out that on rail travel from Calgary to Vancouver it was downhill. There was then a change of freight rates. But British Columbia is in a spot. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I have some indication from the hon. member who is leading the house as to what the business will be on Monday, April 6, when we reconvene? I hope the minister will be in a position to give us as much of the business for the succeeding days as possible.

Mr. Speaker, when the house reassembles on Monday, April 6, it will be
Business of the House
engaged in private members' bills. On Tuesday, April 7, we will proceed with the resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Transport. The second item of business will be second reading of the act to amend the Canada Shipping Act also standing in the name of the Minister of Transport. The third item will be the resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Finance dealing with amendments to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act. That is as far as we can forecast the business of the house. I regret I cannot inform the hon. member with regard to the following days.

It being three minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, until Monday, April 6, 1959, pursuant to the order of the house passed on March 9, 1959.
